newsitem.title: SPAIN: ETA injures four with car-bomb blast on barracks.
newsitem.headline: ETA injures four with car-bomb blast on barracks.

text.p: Spain's Basque separatist group ETA injured four people with a car-bomb attack against Civil Guard barracks on Friday, its biggest strike since August.
The blast showed the rebel group was not yet ready for peace talks with the Spanish government, a conservative politician said.
ETA has staged only minor attacks in the last couple of months, prompting press speculation about the possible reasons for the lull.

"(The attack) will serve as a warning to those who let themselves be seduced by the radical environment and pretend to see changes in ETA's strategy," said Carlos Iturgaiz, head of the ruling Popular Party (PP) in the Basque country.
Friday's victims were slightly injured, in the sixth attack this year by the ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) on paramilitary Civil Guard barracks in the northeastern region of Navarre.

Witnesses said a young man parked a Volkswagen, packed with 40 kg (88 pounds) of explosives, near the barracks in the town of Bunuel shortly after 1.00 a.m. (midnight GMT) and fled in another vehicle.
The parked car exploded shortly afterwards, blasting a ten-metre (yard) hole into the wall of the barracks and injuring three women and a Civil Guard. They did not require hospital treatment.

"We were sleeping in bed and all of a sudden, we heard a terrible noise," said the Civil Guard, a 31-year-old man whose three children were also sleeping in the barracks. "I saw a blast and the window crashed on top of me."

"The first thing I did was to get the children out of bed and bring them down into the street," said the man, who was not identified. "It isn't just luck, it's an authentic miracle (that more people were not injured)," he said.

Three bombs exploded at regional courthouses in northern Spain on October 19 but no one was hurt. Police also blamed ETA for an unexploded parcel bomb sent to Civil Guard barracks in Navarre on October 11.
Leaders of Spain's main political parties assailed a Roman Catholic bishop last month for offering to mediate between the government and the rebels.
Bishop of Bilbao Ricardo Blazquez offered to try to end nearly three decades of violence, echoing similar offers made by other religious leaders.
ETA has killed some 800 people since 1968 in its fight for an independent Basque state and frequently targets security forces and police.
A survey published in August, at the height of a summer campaign of ETA bombings, showed 57 percent of Spaniards supported government talks with the separatists.
But Justice Minister Margarita Mariscal de Gante recently said: "There's no place for mediation between ETA and the government."

There have been no known contacts between ETA and the Spanish administration since last year, when Argentine Nobel Peace laureate Adolfo Perez Esquivel carried out a series of unsuccessful contacts. He kept his efforts secret until June this year.
